title: Constantinople, 1453
hookLine: Mehmed II takes Constantinople, which becomes Istanbul

lines: A HARBOR CLOSED BY A CHAIN.
cards: Ships are moving over a hill. Not sailing around it. Over it.

Oxen strain at ropes, men push from behind, and wooden warships slide across greased timbers laid on the ground, up the slope and down the other side, into a harbor that a great iron chain was supposed to keep closed.
Inside the walls, the defenders wake to find enemy ships on water they thought was safe. The city is Constantinople, the old capital of the Byzantine emperors.
The man who ordered the ships over the hill is a young Ottoman sultan named Mehmed. Today's word: Constantinople.

teach.b: Constantinople sat where Europe meets Asia, on a narrow strait called the Bosphorus, with the Golden Horn harbor on one side. Its land walls had turned back earlier armies, including Muslim ones.
And the city had long been in Muslim imaginations.
A saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, praises the commander and the army who will one day take Constantinople.

Scholars have debated how strong that saying's chain of narrators is, but the Ottomans took it to heart. Mehmed prepared like a builder. He raised a fortress on the European shore of the Bosphorus to control the strait.
He brought great cannons to batter the walls.
When the chain kept his fleet out of the harbor, he moved the ships overland. After a long siege, the walls were breached, and the last Byzantine emperor died in the fighting.
Then came days that need to be told honestly: the city was plundered, and people were killed or carried off into captivity.
Conquest in that age was cruel, and Orthodox Christians still remember the day as the fall of the city. Then Mehmed set about refilling the city.
He brought in Muslims, Christians and Jews from across his lands, and made it his capital.

In time the name Istanbul took hold, though Ottoman documents went on using forms of the old name too. For Muslims it became the seat of an empire; for Orthodox Christians, it remains the city of their ancient patriarch.

how: The conquest is commemorated in Istanbul, while Orthodox Christians remember the same event as the fall of the city; the Ecumenical Patriarchate still has its seat there.

games.q: you're Mehmed. a great iron chain closes the harbor, and your fleet can't get in. what do you do?
o: ram the chain until it breaks.
drag the ships over the hill.
games.why: oxen and men hauled warships over greased timbers, up and over the land, and into the harbor behind the chain.

practice: Open a map of Istanbul, or picture it: a long blue strait running north to south, a curved harbor cutting in from the side, and a city on both shores, one in Europe and one in Asia.
Find the old peninsula where the walls stood, and think of the people inside them, and the people outside. If you pray, you can remember all of them.

wordCard.voice: Constantinople. The Byzantine capital on the Bosphorus, taken by Mehmed after a long siege, and in time called Istanbul. Today's word.
